program_name: Voluntary paid family leave insurance (employer group policies or voluntarily purchased employee policies)
summary: Alabama has no state paid family leave program. A 2023 law lets insurers sell paid family leave policies to employers, so you're covered only if your employer buys one.
wage_replacement: Set by each policy; only if your employer buys coverage (or you buy a voluntary employee policy where one is offered).
waiting_period: Set by each policy (the law only requires the policy to say whether there is an unpaid waiting period).
job_protection: This law does not protect your job. The federal FMLA may: up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if your employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you have worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. We found no state law that adds job-protected leave for private-sector workers.
eligibility: Only workers covered by an employer's group disability policy that includes paid family leave, or who buy a voluntary employee policy; eligibility rules are set by the policy. No state-run program.
law_citation: Paid Family Leave Income Replacement Benefits Act, Ala. Code §§ 27-19-150 to 27-19-160; Act 2023-112 (HB 141, 2023 Regular Session), approved May 4, 2023; effective Aug. 1, 2023
state_leave_laws: No state law beyond federal FMLA was found.
pregnancy_accommodation_law: No state pregnancy accommodation law found as of October 2026. The federal Pregnant Workers Fairness Act covers employers with 15+ employees.
lactation_at_work_law: No state lactation-at-work law found as of October 2026. Federal PUMP Act rules apply.
state_employee_parental_leave: Since July 1, 2025, Alabama gives state, public school and community college employees with 12 straight months on the job 8 weeks of leave at 100% of base pay after a birth, stillbirth or miscarriage (2 weeks for fathers), plus 8 weeks for adopting a child age 3 or younger. Employees must agree in writing to stay at least 8 weeks after the leave ends (Ala. Code § 36-6A-1 et seq.; Act 2025-81, SB 199).
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: Alabama's Paid Family Leave Income Replacement Benefits Act lets disability insurers add paid family leave to employer group policies or sell it as voluntary employee policies, covering reasons such as bonding in the first 12 months after a birth, adoption or foster placement. Policies must pay at least 2 weeks of benefits in a 52-week period. It took effect Aug. 1, 2023 (Ala. Code §§ 27-19-150 to 27-19-160; Act 2023-112, HB 141).

summary: Alaska has no state paid family leave program, so paid time off after birth depends on your employer; federal FMLA gives eligible workers 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave.
wage_replacement: No state paid family leave program.
job_protection: Federal FMLA gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if the employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you've worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. We found no state law that adds job-protected leave for private-sector workers. Alaska's Family Leave Act covers only state and local government employers, not private ones.
state_leave_laws: No state law beyond federal FMLA was found. Alaska's Family Leave Act covers only state and local government employers, not private ones.
pregnancy_accommodation_law: Alaska's law covers only public employers: a pregnant employee of the state or a local government with 21+ employees can ask to transfer to an open, less strenuous or less hazardous job that her health care provider recommends. Private employers aren't covered by a state accommodation law (Alaska Stat. § 39.20.520, 1992).
lactation_at_work_law: No state lactation-at-work law found as of October 2026. A state payroll policy lets state employees pump as needed in a private space that isn't a bathroom (Alaska Administrative Manual 280.460).
state_employee_parental_leave: Alaska state employees can take up to 18 weeks of family leave within 12 months for pregnancy, birth or adoption, compared with 12 weeks under FMLA. Most of it is unpaid: employees must first use accrued paid leave until 5 days remain (Alaska Stat. § 39.20.305). Local governments with 21+ employees must offer the same 18 weeks.
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: No voluntary paid family leave insurance law found as of October 2026.

program_name: Voluntary family leave insurance (employer-purchased)
summary: Arkansas has no state paid family leave program. A 2023 law lets insurers sell paid family leave policies to employers, so you're covered only if your employer buys one.
wage_replacement: Set by each policy; only if your employer buys coverage.
waiting_period: Set by each policy (the law only requires the policy to say whether there is an unpaid waiting period).
job_protection: This law does not protect your job. The federal FMLA may: up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if your employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you have worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. We found no state law that adds job-protected leave for private-sector workers.
eligibility: Only employees whose employer buys a family leave insurance policy or rider; eligibility rules are set by the policy. No state-run program.
law_citation: Ark. Code Ann. § 23-62-112 (Family leave insurance); Act 84 of 2023 (SB 111, 94th General Assembly), approved Feb. 17, 2023
state_leave_laws: No state law beyond federal FMLA was found.
pregnancy_accommodation_law: No state pregnancy accommodation law found as of October 2026. Arkansas's civil rights law bans pregnancy discrimination, and the federal Pregnant Workers Fairness Act covers employers with 15+ employees.
lactation_at_work_law: Arkansas employers must give reasonable unpaid break time each day to pump and make a reasonable effort to provide a private, secure and sanitary place near the work area that isn't a toilet stall. An employer doesn't have to provide break time if it would cause undue hardship (Ark. Code § 11-5-116; Act 621 of 2009).
state_employee_parental_leave: Arkansas state agencies can grant female state employees with 1+ year of service up to 12 consecutive weeks of maternity leave at full pay within 12 weeks of a birth, or of adopting or fostering a baby under 1, without using up sick or annual leave first (Ark. Code § 21-4-214; raised from 4 weeks by Act 770 of 2023). Public school districts and charter schools that opt in offer up to 12 weeks of paid maternity leave, with the state covering the full cost since 2025 (Ark. Code § 6-17-122).
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: Arkansas lets accident and health or life insurers sell family leave insurance to employers, as a rider to or part of a group disability policy or as a separate group policy, to replace part of an employee's pay during leave for a birth, adoption or foster placement, a seriously ill family member, or a family member's military call-up. The law sets no minimum number of weeks or benefit amount (Ark. Code § 23-62-112; Act 84 of 2023, SB 111, approved Feb. 17, 2023).

program_name: California State Disability Insurance (SDI): Disability Insurance (DI) and Paid Family Leave (PFL)
summary: California pays new moms through State Disability Insurance (usually up to 4 weeks before and 6 to 8 weeks after birth), then up to 8 weeks of Paid Family Leave to bond, at 70% to 90% of wages up to $1,765 a week in 2026.
pregnancy_recovery_typical: EDD says pregnancy Disability Insurance usually lasts 10 to 12 weeks: up to 4 weeks before your due date and up to 6 weeks after a vaginal birth or 8 weeks after a C-section. Your doctor or midwife can certify longer if there are complications. After your last DI payment, EDD sends you a PFL New Mother claim (DE 2501FP) so you can add up to 8 weeks of bonding.
wage_replacement: About 70% to 90% of the wages you earned 5 to 18 months before your claim, based on your highest-earning quarter: 90% for lower earners, and for higher earners 70% (or a flat $1,127 in one middle band, per EDD's table). $50/week minimum, $1,765/week maximum in 2026. DI and PFL use the same formula and max.
waiting_period: 7-day unpaid waiting period for Disability Insurance (pregnancy/childbirth); no waiting period for PFL bonding.
job_protection: SDI and PFL do not protect your job; EDD says they pay benefits only. Job protection comes from other laws. California Pregnancy Disability Leave (PDL) gives up to 4 months of job-protected leave for pregnancy disability at employers with 5 or more employees, with no tenure or hours requirement. CFRA gives up to 12 weeks of job-protected bonding leave at employers with 5 or more employees if you have worked there at least 12 months and 1,250 hours. Federal FMLA covers employers with 50 or more employees within 75 miles. PDL and CFRA bonding leave are separate, so PDL runs first and CFRA bonding runs after.
eligibility: You need at least $300 in wages with SDI withheld ("CASDI" on your paystub) in your base period, about 5 to 18 months before your claim. You must be employed or actively looking for work when the leave starts, and you must lose wages. For DI you must be unable to do your regular work for at least 8 days and be certified by a licensed health professional; a licensed midwife or nurse-midwife can certify normal pregnancy and postpartum. There is no minimum hours or job-tenure test. Citizenship and immigration status don't affect eligibility. Self-employed people can buy Disability Insurance Elective Coverage (DIEC). Some public employees are not covered.

program_name: Colorado Paid Family and Medical Leave Insurance (FAMLI)
summary: Colorado pays up to 12 weeks for pregnancy and bonding combined (16 with a pregnancy or childbirth complication), at up to 90% of wages, max $1,448.02 a week from July 1, 2026.
pregnancy_recovery_typical: FAMLI says most birthing parents file a Pregnancy Leave claim first (once a health care provider certifies the need), then a separate Bonding Leave claim after the birth. Both come out of the same 12-week balance, unless your provider certifies a pregnancy or childbirth complication, which uses a separate 4-week balance (up to 16 weeks) and can continue after the baby is born.
wage_replacement: 90% of your average weekly wage up to half the state average weekly wage, plus 50% of wages above that. Max $1,448.02/week from July 1, 2026 ($1,381.45 earlier in 2026).
waiting_period: None
job_protection: Yes, in the FAMLI Act itself: if you have worked for your employer at least 180 days before leave, you have the right to return to your job or an equivalent one with equivalent pay and benefits. Health insurance continues during leave, and retaliation is banned for everyone. If your local government employer opted out of FAMLI and you opted in yourself, your job is not protected by FAMLI, though federal FMLA may apply.
eligibility: Most Colorado employees qualify after earning $2,500 in Colorado wages subject to FAMLI premiums in the last 5 completed calendar quarters; there is no minimum time with your current employer. Private employers and state government are covered; local governments can opt out. Self-employed and gig workers (and employees of opted-out local governments) can opt in for at least 3 years.

program_name: Connecticut Paid Leave (CT Paid Family and Medical Leave Insurance Program)
summary: Connecticut pays up to 12 weeks for pregnancy, recovery and bonding combined (14 with a serious pregnancy complication), at up to 95% of wages, max $1,016.40 a week in 2026.
pregnancy_recovery_typical: CT Paid Leave covers prenatal appointments, pregnancy complications, childbirth and the post-delivery 'recovery period' your provider certifies. It sets no standard number of weeks. Pregnancy, recovery and bonding all come out of the same 12 weeks, plus up to 2 extra weeks (14 total) if you have a serious health condition during pregnancy.
wage_replacement: 95% of your average weekly wage up to 40 times the CT minimum wage ($677.60 in 2026), plus 60% of the amount above that. Capped at 60 times the minimum wage: $1,016.40/week in 2026.
waiting_period: None.
job_protection: CT Paid Leave itself does not protect your job; it only replaces income. Job protection comes from the CT Family and Medical Leave Act, which covers almost all employers with 1+ employee in CT (not municipalities or the federal government). You qualify after 3 months with your employer, with no hours requirement. It gives 12 weeks plus 2 for pregnancy incapacity. Federal FMLA (50+ employees, 12 months, 1,250 hours) may also apply. You request job-protected leave from your employer separately from your CT Paid Leave claim.
eligibility: You must be working for a covered CT employer now, or have worked for one in the last 12 weeks, and have earned at least $2,325 from covered employers in your highest-earning quarter of the base period (first 4 of the last 5 completed quarters). Most private employers with 1+ CT employee are covered. Self-employed people and sole proprietors can enroll. Bonding must be used within 12 months of the birth.

program_name: Delaware Paid Leave (Delaware Paid Family and Medical Leave Insurance Program)
summary: Delaware pays 80% of wages, up to $900 a week, for up to 12 weeks to bond and up to 6 weeks of medical leave, 12 weeks combined. Benefits started January 1, 2026; you need 12 months and 1,250 hours with an employer of 10+ workers.
wage_replacement: 80% of your average weekly wages over the prior 12 months; min $100/week (or your full wage if you earn less); max $900/week in 2026 and 2027.
waiting_period: None in the law (no unpaid waiting week). DDOL says the first payment takes about two weeks to process after approval (anti-fraud review), then payments are weekly.
job_protection: Yes, in the Paid Leave law: covered employees must be restored to the same job or one with equivalent seniority, status, pay and benefits, and health coverage continues during leave. You only qualify (and are protected) after 12 months and 1,250 hours with your current employer, and only if that employer has 10+ employees in Delaware (10-24 employees: parental leave only).
eligibility: You must work primarily in Delaware, for an employer with at least 10 Delaware employees, and have worked for that employer at least 12 months and 1,250 hours (about 25 hours/week) in the last 12 months. Employers with 10-24 employees only have to provide parental (bonding) leave; 25+ employees must also provide medical, family caregiving and military leave. Part-time or short-term workers may be put on a waiver and excluded. No self-employed opt-in found in the law.

program_name: District of Columbia Paid Family Leave (Universal Paid Leave Amendment Act)
summary: DC pays up to 12 weeks of parental leave to bond plus 2 weeks of prenatal leave, at up to 90% of wages, max $1,100 a week for claims filed from October 1, 2026.
pregnancy_recovery_typical: DC gives up to 2 weeks of prenatal leave during pregnancy, in full-day increments for prenatal appointments, pregnancy treatment or doctor-ordered bed rest. After the birth you get up to 12 weeks of parental (bonding) leave, so up to 14 weeks total around the birth. Medical leave covers pregnancy complications or stillbirth, but it counts toward the same 12-week yearly cap.
wage_replacement: 90% of your average weekly wage up to 150% of DC's minimum wage times 40 hours, plus 50% of the amount above that. Max $1,100/week for applications filed on or after October 1, 2026 ($1,190/week for applications filed October 1, 2025 to September 30, 2026).
waiting_period: None (the one-week waiting period was eliminated for claims filed on or after July 25, 2022).
job_protection: DC Paid Family Leave does not protect your job, but it does prohibit retaliation, enforced by the DC Office of Human Rights. Job protection comes from the DC Family and Medical Leave Act: employers with 20+ employees, for workers employed 1 year and 1,000 hours in the past 12 months, with up to 16 weeks of family leave and 16 weeks of medical leave in 24 months. Federal FMLA may also apply. Per the official notice, workers at employers with fewer than 20 employees have no job protection when taking DC PFL.
eligibility: You must be a covered employee of a private-sector DC employer, generally spending more than half your work time in DC, with wages your employer reported to DC for unemployment insurance. Coverage must be for some or all of the 52 weeks before your qualifying event, and you must be currently employed when you apply. DC government, federal government and WMATA employees are not covered (the OPFL questionnaire also lists religious institutions). Self-employed people who work more than half the time in DC can opt in. Apply within 30 days after the event; you can't apply before it happens.

eligibility: Only employees whose employer buys a paid family leave insurance policy or rider; eligibility rules are set by the policy. No state-run program.
law_citation: Fla. Stat. §§ 624.6086 and 627.445; ch. 2023-149, Laws of Florida (CS/CS/HB 721), approved May 25, 2023; effective upon becoming law (May 25, 2023)
state_leave_laws: No Florida law requires employers to give maternity leave. The Florida Civil Rights Act makes it illegal for employers with 15 or more employees to fire you, refuse to hire you, or treat you worse in pay or other terms of employment because of pregnancy (Fla. Stat. §§ 760.02(7) and 760.10; pregnancy added in 2015). Complaints go to the Florida Commission on Human Relations.
pregnancy_accommodation_law: No state pregnancy accommodation law found as of October 2026. Florida's Civil Rights Act bans pregnancy discrimination, but accommodation requests fall under the federal PWFA, which the EEOC enforces.
lactation_at_work_law: No state lactation-at-work law found as of October 2026. Federal PUMP Act rules apply.
state_employee_parental_leave: Florida gives eligible State Personnel System employees up to 7 weeks of paid maternity leave right after giving birth, plus up to 2 weeks of paid bonding leave within a year of a birth or adoption, after a year of service and 1,250 hours worked in the past 12 months (Fla. Admin. Code R. 60L-34.00421, effective Dec. 11, 2023). Career service employees can also take up to 6 months of unpaid parental leave and return to the same or an equivalent job (Fla. Stat. § 110.221).
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: A 2023 law lets insurers sell paid family leave insurance to employers, as a group policy or a rider to group disability coverage, with at least 2 weeks of benefits per covered reason in a year. You're covered only if your employer buys it (Fla. Stat. §§ 624.6086 and 627.445; ch. 2023-149, effective May 25, 2023).

summary: Georgia has no state paid family leave program, so paid time off after birth depends on your employer; federal FMLA gives eligible workers 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave.
wage_replacement: No state paid family leave program.
job_protection: Federal FMLA gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if the employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you've worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. We found no state law that adds job-protected leave for private-sector workers.
state_leave_laws: No Georgia law requires employers to give maternity leave. Georgia's Family Care Act lets employees who work 30 or more hours a week, at employers with 25 or more employees (including state and local government) that provide paid sick leave, use up to 5 days a year of earned sick leave to care for an immediate family member such as a child. It doesn't require employers to offer sick leave, and employers with an employee stock ownership plan are exempt (O.C.G.A. § 34-1-10, 2017; made permanent by Act 90 of 2023).
pregnancy_accommodation_law: No state pregnancy accommodation law found as of October 2026. Federal PWFA rules apply.
lactation_at_work_law: Georgia requires employers with one or more employees to give reasonable break time to pump at work, paid at the employee's regular rate, and a private place other than a restroom. Employers with fewer than 50 employees are excused where this would cause undue hardship, and state and local government employers aren't covered by this law (O.C.G.A. § 34-1-6).
state_employee_parental_leave: Georgia gives full-time executive-branch state employees up to 240 hours (6 weeks at 40 hours a week) of paid parental leave in a 12-month period for a birth, adoption or foster placement. Employees who give birth also get up to 120 hours (3 weeks) of paid maternal birth leave in the 3 weeks after delivery. Salaried staff qualify after 6 months on the job and hourly staff after 700 hours in 6 months (O.C.G.A. §§ 45-20-17 and 45-20-23; State Personnel Board Rule 478-1-.16, revised Aug. 2026). The same paid parental leave law also covers full-time public school employees through their local boards of education (O.C.G.A. § 45-20-17, Act 225 of 2021).
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: No voluntary paid family leave insurance law found as of October 2026.

program_name: Hawaii Temporary Disability Insurance (TDI): employer-provided disability pay for off-the-job illness or injury, including pregnancy and childbirth. Hawaii has no state paid family or bonding leave.
summary: Hawaii has no paid leave to bond, but Temporary Disability Insurance pays 58% of wages (max $871 a week in 2026) for up to 26 weeks while you recover from pregnancy and childbirth.
wage_replacement: TDI only (statutory plan): 58% of your average weekly wage, rounded up to the next dollar, max $871/week in 2026, for up to 26 weeks while a doctor certifies you can't work, including pregnancy and childbirth recovery. Approved employer plans may pay differently. No paid bonding leave.
waiting_period: 7 consecutive days for TDI under a statutory plan (benefits start on the 8th day of disability); approved employer plans may differ
job_protection: TDI itself does not protect your job. The Hawaii Family Leave Law (HRS ch. 398) gives up to 4 weeks a year of job-protected family leave, including for the birth of a child, if your employer has 100+ employees in Hawaii and you've worked there 6 consecutive months. That leave is unpaid unless you use accrued leave, and you can use up to 10 days of accrued sick leave for it. Federal FMLA (50+ employees, 12 months/1,250 hours) may also apply.
eligibility: To get TDI you must have at least 14 weeks of Hawaii employment in which you were paid for 20+ hours, have earned at least $400 in the 52 weeks before the disability, and be in current employment (or have left work no more than 2 weeks before the disability began). Your disability, including pregnancy, must be certified by a provider. Employers must provide the coverage; some workers (e.g., federal employees, commission-only real estate and insurance agents) are excluded.
state_leave_laws: Hawaii's Family Leave Law gives up to 4 weeks a year of unpaid, job-protected leave, including for the birth of a child, if your employer has 100+ employees in Hawaii and you've worked there 6 consecutive months. You can use up to 10 days of accrued sick leave during it.

summary: Illinois has no state paid family leave program, so paid time off after birth depends on your employer; federal FMLA gives eligible workers 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave.
wage_replacement: No state paid family leave program.
job_protection: Federal FMLA gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if the employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you've worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. Illinois' Human Rights Act (all employers) requires reasonable pregnancy accommodations, which can include leave needed for pregnancy or childbirth and time off to recover, with return to the same or an equivalent job unless that causes undue hardship. FMLA-eligible workers also get up to 10 unpaid workdays after a miscarriage or stillbirth.
state_leave_laws: Illinois' Human Rights Act (all employers) requires reasonable pregnancy accommodations, which can include leave needed for pregnancy or childbirth and time off to recover, with return to the same or an equivalent job unless that causes undue hardship. FMLA-eligible workers also get up to 10 unpaid workdays after a miscarriage or stillbirth.
pregnancy_accommodation_law: Illinois requires employers of any size, public and private, to make reasonable accommodations for pregnancy, childbirth and related conditions unless that would cause undue hardship. Accommodations can include more breaks, light duty, a private space to pump and time off to recover, with return to the same or an equivalent job (775 ILCS 5/2-102(J), in effect since 2015).
lactation_at_work_law: Illinois requires employers with more than 5 employees, including state and local government, to give paid break time at the employee's regular rate to pump for one year after birth, unless that would cause undue hardship. They must also make reasonable efforts to provide a private room near the work area, other than a toilet stall (Nursing Mothers in the Workplace Act, 820 ILCS 260, break-time section last amended effective Jan. 1, 2026).
state_employee_parental_leave: Illinois gives state employees under the Personnel Code 10 weeks (50 workdays) of paid parental leave for a birth or adoption, taken in full-week blocks, and both parents get it if both work for the state (80 Ill. Adm. Code 303.130, as amended in 2019). Employees also get 5 weeks of paid leave after a stillbirth (303.131).
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: No voluntary paid family leave insurance law found as of October 2026.

Code 22-9-12, 2021). Executive-branch state employees get reasonable accommodations under a state personnel policy (Executive Order 21-10).

Code 22-2-14, 2008). State and local government employers must also give reasonable paid break time each day (Ind. Code 5-10-6-2).

New parents in those agencies, including through adoption or foster care, also get up to 150 paid hours (75 for part-time staff) to use within 6 months (Executive Order 17-31, 2017).

Iowa's Civil Rights Act requires employers with 4+ employees to grant leave for the time a worker is disabled by pregnancy, childbirth or related conditions, up to 8 weeks, when their leave plans don't cover it. state_leave_laws: Iowa's Civil Rights Act requires employers with 4+ employees to grant leave for the time a worker is disabled by pregnancy, childbirth or related conditions, up to 8 weeks, when their leave plans don't cover it. Give timely notice; the employer may require medical certification. Firing someone because of pregnancy is illegal.
pregnancy_accommodation_law: No state pregnancy accommodation law found as of October 2026. Iowa's Civil Rights Act does require employers with 4+ employees to grant up to 8 weeks of leave for pregnancy-related disability when their leave plans don't cover it.
lactation_at_work_law: No state lactation-at-work law found as of October 2026. Federal PUMP Act rules apply.
state_employee_parental_leave: Iowa gives state employees up to 4 weeks of paid leave after giving birth or adopting, and up to 1 week for a parent who didn't give birth, to use within 12 months (Iowa Code § 70A.24, 2025). Since April 30, 2026, employees no longer have to be FMLA-eligible to get it.
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: No voluntary paid family leave insurance law found as of October 2026. Bills for a state family and medical leave insurance program (HF 2631, SF 2239) didn't pass in 2026.

summary: Kansas has no state paid family leave program, so paid time off after birth depends on your employer; federal FMLA gives eligible workers 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave.
wage_replacement: No state paid family leave program.
job_protection: Federal FMLA gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if the employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you've worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. Kansas Human Rights Commission rules require employers with 4+ employees to treat childbearing as a valid reason for a leave of absence of a 'reasonable' length. A mother who says she'll return within a reasonable time must get her job, or one of like status and pay, back without losing seniority or benefits.
state_leave_laws: Kansas Human Rights Commission rules require employers with 4+ employees to treat childbearing as a valid reason for a leave of absence of a 'reasonable' length. A mother who says she'll return within a reasonable time must get her job, or one of like status and pay, back without losing seniority or benefits.
pregnancy_accommodation_law: No state pregnancy accommodation law found as of October 2026. Kansas Human Rights Commission rules do require employers with 4+ employees to allow a reasonable leave of absence for childbearing.
lactation_at_work_law: No state lactation-at-work law found as of October 2026. Federal PUMP Act rules apply.
state_employee_parental_leave: Kansas gives executive-branch state employees paid parental leave at 100% pay after a birth, adoption or foster placement: 8 weeks for the primary caregiver and 4 weeks for the secondary caregiver (Executive Order 21-24, 2021). Employees hired on or after July 6, 2021 must work 180 days first.
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: No voluntary paid family leave insurance law found as of October 2026.

program_name: Voluntary paid family leave insurance (employer-purchased)
summary: Kentucky has no state paid family leave program. A 2024 law lets insurers sell paid family leave policies to employers, so you're covered only if your employer buys one.
wage_replacement: Set by each policy; only if your employer buys coverage.
waiting_period: Set by each policy (the law only requires the policy to say whether there is an unpaid waiting period).
job_protection: This law does not protect your job. The federal FMLA may: up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if your employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you have worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. Kentucky's Pregnant Workers Act requires employers with 15+ workers to give reasonable accommodations, which can include time off to recover from childbirth, unless it causes undue hardship. No set length or pay. Separately, every employer must grant up to 6 weeks of leave, on written request, to adopt a child under 10.
eligibility: Only employees whose employer buys a paid family leave insurance policy or rider; eligibility rules are set by the policy. No state-run program.
law_citation: Paid Family Leave Insurance Act, KRS 304.53-010 to 304.53-070; 2024 Ky. Acts ch. 99 (HB 179, 2024 Regular Session), signed and effective April 5, 2024 (emergency clause)
state_leave_laws: Kentucky's Pregnant Workers Act requires employers with 15+ workers to give reasonable accommodations, which can include time off to recover from childbirth, unless it causes undue hardship. No set length or pay. Separately, every employer must grant up to 6 weeks of leave, on written request, to adopt a child under 10.
pregnancy_accommodation_law: Kentucky's Pregnant Workers Act (2019) requires employers with 15+ employees in the state to make reasonable accommodations for pregnancy, childbirth and related conditions unless it causes undue hardship. Examples in the law include more frequent or longer breaks, time off to recover from childbirth, seating, light duty, a temporary transfer and a modified schedule (KRS 344.030, 344.040).
lactation_at_work_law: Kentucky's Pregnant Workers Act counts lactation as a pregnancy-related condition, so employers with 15+ employees must provide reasonable accommodations such as extra breaks and a private space that isn't a bathroom to pump, unless it causes undue hardship (KRS 344.030, 344.040; 2019). Federal PUMP Act rules also apply.
state_employee_parental_leave: Kentucky's personnel rules give full-time state employees in the classified and unclassified services up to 6 weeks of continuous employer-paid leave for a birth and newborn care within a year, an adoption or foster placement, or their own serious health condition, available from the first day on the job. The 6 weeks are one shared allotment that renews after 10 and 20 years of service (101 KAR 2:102 and 101 KAR 3:015, current versions effective Sept. 30, 2025).
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: Kentucky's Paid Family Leave Insurance Act lets insurers sell paid family leave coverage to employers as part of, or a rider to, a group disability policy, or as a stand-alone group policy. Covered reasons can include bonding in the first 12 months after a birth, adoption or foster placement, and policies must pay at least 2 weeks for each covered reason in a 52-week period (KRS 304.53-010 to 304.53-070; HB 179, effective April 5, 2024).

summary: Louisiana has no state paid family leave program. A 2026 law lets insurers sell paid family leave policies to employers, so you're covered only if your employer buys one.
wage_replacement: Set by each policy; only if your employer buys coverage.
waiting_period: Set by each policy (the policy may set an unpaid waiting period).
job_protection: This law does not protect your job. The federal FMLA may: up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if your employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you have worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. Louisiana requires employers with more than 25 workers to allow pregnancy leave: 6 weeks for a normal pregnancy and childbirth, or the time you are disabled by pregnancy or childbirth, up to 4 months. The law does not require pay, but you may use accrued annual leave. Your employer may require reasonable notice.
eligibility: Only employees whose employer buys a paid family leave insurance policy or rider; eligibility rules are set by the policy. No state-run program.
law_citation: Paid Family Leave Insurance Act, La. R.S. 22:1192.1-1192.4; Act No. 817 of the 2026 Regular Session (HB 591, Rep. Kyle M. Green Jr.), signed June 8, 2026
state_leave_laws: Louisiana requires employers with more than 25 workers to allow pregnancy leave: 6 weeks for a normal pregnancy and childbirth, or the time you are disabled by pregnancy or childbirth, up to 4 months. The law does not require pay, but you may use accrued annual leave. Your employer may require reasonable notice.
pregnancy_accommodation_law: Since 2021, Louisiana employers with more than 25 employees must make reasonable accommodations for limitations from pregnancy, childbirth or related conditions unless it causes undue hardship, and can't make you take leave if another accommodation would work. Employers must also give employees written notice of these rights (La. R.S. 23:341-342; Act 393 of 2021).
lactation_at_work_law: Louisiana requires every public school board to give school employees a private room other than a restroom and reasonable break time to pump for up to 1 year after birth; break time beyond existing breaks is unpaid (La. R.S. 17:81(W)). Private employers have no lactation-specific state law, though A Better Balance reads the pregnancy accommodation law (employers with more than 25 employees) to cover pumping breaks and space.
state_employee_parental_leave: Louisiana's classified state employees get up to 240 hours (6 weeks full time) of paid parental leave at 100% of base pay for a child born, adopted or placed in foster care on or after Jan. 1, 2024, used within 12 weeks of the event. You need 12 months of state service and 1,250 hours worked in the past year (Civil Service Rule 11.36). A 2026 law (Act 744) adds 6 weeks at full pay for public school employees, subject to legislative funding.
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: Louisiana's Paid Family Leave Insurance Act lets life and disability income insurers sell paid family leave insurance as a stand-alone policy or a rider, covering a birth, adoption or foster placement, care for a seriously ill family member, and military needs. Policies must pay at least 2 weeks in a 52-week period and may have an unpaid waiting period. It took effect June 8, 2026 (La. R.S. 22:1192.1-1192.4; Act 817 of 2026, HB 591).

program_name: Maine Paid Family and Medical Leave (PFML)
summary: Maine pays up to 12 weeks a year for pregnancy recovery and bonding combined, at up to 90% of wages, max $1,249.12 a week from July 1, 2026. Benefits started May 1, 2026.
wage_replacement: 90% of your average weekly wage up to half the state average weekly wage, plus 66% of wages above that, capped at the state average weekly wage: $1,249.12/week from July 1, 2026 (Maine DOL rounds it to $1,250); $1,198.84 for May-June 2026.
waiting_period: 7 calendar days for medical leave, once per benefit year (you can use PTO during it); none for bonding and other family leave
job_protection: Yes, in the PFML law: if you've worked for your employer at least 120 consecutive days, you must be restored to your job or an equivalent one with equivalent pay, benefits and conditions. Under 120 days, your employer may restore you but doesn't have to. Retaliation is banned for everyone. PFML runs at the same time as federal FMLA and Maine family medical leave when they apply.
eligibility: You must have earned at least 6 times the state average weekly wage (about $7,190 at the 2025-26 rate, about $7,495 at the July 2026 rate) in Maine during your base period, the first 4 of the last 5 completed calendar quarters. Covers almost everyone employed in Maine, whatever the employer's size. Self-employed people can opt in. Federal employees aren't covered, and Tribal government employees aren't unless the Tribe opts in.

program_name: Maryland Family and Medical Leave Insurance (FAMLI)
summary: Maryland passed paid family and medical leave, but benefits don't start until January 2028: up to 12 weeks (24 with both recovery and bonding) at up to 90% of wages, max $1,000 a week.
wage_replacement: When benefits start in January 2028: 90% of your average weekly wage up to 65% of the state average weekly wage, plus 50% of wages above that; min $50, max $1,000/week through Dec. 31, 2028, CPI-adjusted after that. No benefits are paid in 2026.
waiting_period: None (benefits from the first day of leave)
job_protection: Yes, in the FAMLI law: when leave ends, your employer must restore you to an equivalent position, and during leave can fire you only for cause. The only exception is if denying restoration is needed to prevent 'substantial and grievous economic injury' to the employer, the employer gives notice, and you then choose not to return. There is no separate job-tenure test beyond FAMLI's 680-hour eligibility rule. FAMLI runs at the same time as federal FMLA when both apply.
eligibility: Once benefits start, you'll need to have worked at least 680 hours in a Maryland-based job in the 4 reported calendar quarters before you apply or your leave begins (hours can come from more than one employer). There is no minimum earnings test. Covers employees of employers of any size; employers with fewer than 15 employees don't pay the employer share. Federal employees aren't covered. Self-employed Marylanders will be able to opt in later.

program_name: Massachusetts Paid Family and Medical Leave (PFML)
summary: Massachusetts pays up to 20 weeks of medical leave for pregnancy and recovery plus 12 weeks to bond, capped at 26 weeks a year, at up to 80% of wages, max $1,230.39 a week in 2026.
pregnancy_recovery_typical: DFML sets no standard number of weeks: your health care provider decides how much medical leave you need for pregnancy complications and recovery after childbirth (up to 20 weeks). DFML's examples include 6 weeks of prenatal bed rest plus 8 weeks of recovery, or 10 weeks of recovery after birth. You can then add up to 12 weeks of bonding, within a 26-week yearly cap.
wage_replacement: 80% of your individual average weekly wage up to half the state average weekly wage ($1,922.48 in 2026), plus 50% of the amount above that. Max $1,230.39/week for benefit years starting in 2026 (64% of the state average); $1,284.61 in 2027. Your rate is set for your whole 52-week benefit year.
waiting_period: 7 calendar days, unpaid, counted against your leave. It's waived when bonding leave immediately follows medical leave for pregnancy or childbirth recovery, so add bonding to the same application.
job_protection: Yes, the PFML law itself protects your job. When you return, your employer must restore you to the same or an equivalent position with the same status, pay, benefits, length-of-service credit and seniority, and must keep your health insurance during leave. The law has no tenure or employer-size test for covered employees. Exceptions: layoffs of comparable coworkers, or a term or project job that ended. Any negative change during leave or within 6 months after is presumed retaliation. This applies even if your employer uses a private plan. The Massachusetts Parental Leave Act may also apply.
eligibility: Most Massachusetts employees are covered. You must have earned at least the DUA minimum ($6,300 currently) in the last 4 completed calendar quarters, and at least 30 times your weekly benefit amount. Self-employed people can opt in through MassTaxConnect, for at least 3 years. Municipal employees are covered only if their employer opts in. If your employer has an approved private plan, you apply through that plan instead of DFML.

summary: Michigan has no state paid family leave program, so paid time off after birth depends on your employer; federal FMLA gives eligible workers 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave.
wage_replacement: No state paid family leave program.
job_protection: Federal FMLA gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if the employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you've worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. We found no state law that adds job-protected leave for private-sector workers. Michigan's civil rights law only requires employers to treat pregnancy and childbirth like other conditions affecting ability to work, including under their leave policies.
state_leave_laws: No state law beyond federal FMLA was found. Michigan's civil rights law only requires employers to treat pregnancy and childbirth like other conditions affecting ability to work, including under their leave policies.
pregnancy_accommodation_law: Michigan has no pregnancy accommodation law for private employers. Civil Service Commission rules require state agencies to accommodate known limitations from pregnancy, childbirth or related conditions for classified state employees, consistent with state and federal law (Civil Service Rule 1-8.2, last amended 2023).
lactation_at_work_law: No state lactation-at-work law found as of October 2026. Federal PUMP Act rules apply.
state_employee_parental_leave: Michigan gives classified state employees 12 weeks of paid parental leave at base pay for a birth or adoption on or after Oct. 1, 2020, once they've finished probation and worked 1,250 hours in the past year. Total parental leave can run up to 6 months, with the time beyond paid leave unpaid (Civil Service Regulation 2.03).
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: No voluntary paid family leave insurance law found as of October 2026.

program_name: Minnesota Paid Leave (Paid Family and Medical Leave)
summary: Minnesota pays up to 12 weeks of pregnancy-related medical leave and 12 weeks to bond, 20 weeks combined, at up to 90% of wages, max $1,423 a week in 2026. Benefits started January 1, 2026.
pregnancy_recovery_typical: Up to 12 weeks of Pregnancy-related Medical Leave, as long as your provider certifies; DEED's examples use 6 weeks of recovery after birth, or 8 weeks after a C-section, followed by 12 weeks of Bonding Leave (up to 20 weeks total). Take the medical leave first, then bonding.
wage_replacement: 90% of wages up to half the state average weekly wage, 66% of wages between half and 100% of it, and 55% of wages above it; max $1,423/week (the state average weekly wage) in 2026.
waiting_period: None (but except for bonding, a claim must be based on a single qualifying event lasting at least 7 calendar days)
job_protection: Yes, in the Paid Leave law: you must be restored to your job or an equivalent position. Job protection generally starts 90 days after your date of hire, but DEED says Pregnancy-related Medical Leave and Bonding Leave are protected no matter how long you've worked there. Retaliation is banned from day one. Federal FMLA, Minnesota's Pregnancy and Parental Leave Act and Earned Sick and Safe Time may add protections and may run at the same time.
eligibility: You must have earned at least 5.3% of the state's average annual wage in the past year (about $3,900 right now), from one or more Minnesota jobs. Covers nearly all Minnesota workers, including full-time, part-time, temporary and most seasonal workers, at employers of any size. Self-employed people, independent contractors and Tribal Nations can opt in. Federal, postal and railroad workers can't; designated seasonal hospitality jobs are excluded.

summary: Mississippi has no state paid family leave program, so paid time off after birth depends on your employer; federal FMLA gives eligible workers 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave.
wage_replacement: No state paid family leave program.
job_protection: Federal FMLA gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if the employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you've worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. We found no state law that adds job-protected leave for private-sector workers.
state_leave_laws: No state law beyond federal FMLA was found.
pregnancy_accommodation_law: No state pregnancy accommodation law found as of October 2026. Federal Pregnant Workers Fairness Act rules apply.
lactation_at_work_law: Mississippi bars employers from stopping an employee from pumping during meal or other breaks the employer already provides, but it doesn't require extra break time or a private space (Miss. Code § 71-1-55, 2006). A separate law has the Health Department require licensed child care centers to give breastfeeding mothers, including staff, a sanitary place that isn't a toilet stall.
state_employee_parental_leave: Since January 1, 2026, Mississippi gives state employees who are a new child's primary caregiver 6 weeks of paid parental leave at 100% of salary after a birth or adoption, to be used within 12 weeks. Employees need 12 months of full-time service, and may then use up to 6 weeks of earned major medical leave (HB 1063, 2025).
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: No voluntary paid family leave insurance law found as of October 2026.

wage_replacement: No state paid family leave program.
job_protection: Federal FMLA gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if the employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you've worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. We found no state law that adds job-protected leave for private-sector workers. Missouri's labor department says an employer must hold a job during maternity leave only under FMLA, or if it holds jobs open for other temporary medical problems.
state_leave_laws: No state law beyond federal FMLA was found. Missouri's labor department says an employer must hold a job during maternity leave only under FMLA, or if it holds jobs open for other temporary medical problems.
pregnancy_accommodation_law: No state pregnancy accommodation law found as of October 2026. State rules require employers to treat pregnancy-related disabilities like other temporary disabilities.
lactation_at_work_law: Missouri requires public school districts to give lactating employees and teachers at least 3 chances each school day to pump and a lockable private room (not a restroom) near a sink and refrigerator, for at least a year after birth. Other employers aren't covered by a state law (Mo. Rev. Stat. 160.995, 2021).
state_employee_parental_leave: Missouri gives executive-branch state employees 6 weeks of parental leave at full pay after a birth or adoption if they're the primary caregiver, or 3 weeks if they're the secondary caregiver. It must be taken within 12 weeks (Executive Order 17-09, 2017).
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: No voluntary paid family leave insurance law found as of October 2026.

summary: Montana has no state paid family leave program, so paid time off after birth depends on your employer; federal FMLA gives eligible workers 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave.
wage_replacement: No state paid family leave program.
job_protection: Federal FMLA gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if the employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you've worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. Montana's Maternity Leave Act covers nearly all employers: they can't fire a worker for being pregnant or refuse a reasonable leave of absence for pregnancy. She can use accrued disability or leave benefits, and must get her job or an equivalent one back unless a private employer's circumstances make that impossible or unreasonable.
state_leave_laws: Montana's Maternity Leave Act covers nearly all employers: they can't fire a worker for being pregnant or refuse a reasonable leave of absence for pregnancy. She can use accrued disability or leave benefits, and must get her job or an equivalent one back unless a private employer's circumstances make that impossible or unreasonable.
pregnancy_accommodation_law: No state pregnancy accommodation law found as of October 2026. Montana's Maternity Leave Act does require all employers to grant a reasonable leave of absence for pregnancy (MCA 49-2-310).
lactation_at_work_law: Montana's law covers only public employers: state and county governments, cities, school districts and the university system must give reasonable unpaid break time to pump and make reasonable efforts to provide a private space near the work area that isn't a toilet stall. Private employers aren't covered (MCA 39-2-215 to 39-2-217, 2007).
state_employee_parental_leave: No state-employee paid parental leave law found as of October 2026. Executive-branch policy gives unpaid maternity leave (at least 6 weeks after birth) and up to 15 working days of unpaid parental leave for fathers and adoptive parents, which employees can cover with accrued leave.
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: No voluntary paid family leave insurance law found as of October 2026.

summary: Nebraska has no state paid family leave program, so paid time off after birth depends on your employer; federal FMLA gives eligible workers 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave.
wage_replacement: No state paid family leave program.
job_protection: Federal FMLA gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if the employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you've worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. Nebraska's Fair Employment Practice Act requires employers with 15+ employees to reasonably accommodate pregnancy, and the law lists time off to recover from childbirth and modified work schedules as accommodations, unless they cause undue hardship. No set number of weeks is guaranteed.
state_leave_laws: Nebraska's Fair Employment Practice Act requires employers with 15+ employees to reasonably accommodate pregnancy, and the law lists time off to recover from childbirth and modified work schedules as accommodations, unless they cause undue hardship. No set number of weeks is guaranteed.
pregnancy_accommodation_law: Nebraska requires employers with 15+ employees, including state and local governments, to make reasonable accommodations for pregnancy, childbirth and related conditions unless that would cause undue hardship. Examples in the law include more frequent breaks, light duty, modified schedules and time off to recover from childbirth (Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 48-1102, 48-1107.02, 2015).
lactation_at_work_law: Nebraska's pregnancy accommodation law lists break time and appropriate facilities for breastfeeding or pumping as reasonable accommodations, so employers with 15+ employees must provide them unless that would cause undue hardship (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 48-1102, 2015). The law sets no minimum break length or end date.
state_employee_parental_leave: Since July 1, 2025, Nebraska gives state employees who give birth 6 weeks (240 hours) of paid maternity leave alongside approved FMLA leave. It covers employees under the state's union contracts and its classified personnel rules, and applies only to mothers who gave birth.
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: No voluntary paid family leave insurance law found as of October 2026.

summary: Nevada has no state paid family leave program, so paid time off after birth depends on your employer; federal FMLA gives eligible workers 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave.
wage_replacement: No state paid family leave program.
job_protection: Federal FMLA gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if the employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you've worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. No standalone maternity leave law. Nevada's Pregnant Workers' Fairness Act (employers with 15+ employees) requires any paid or unpaid sick or disability leave an employer offers to cover pregnancy and childbirth, usable before and after birth or miscarriage. Employers must also discuss accommodations such as a modified schedule.
state_leave_laws: No standalone maternity leave law. Nevada's Pregnant Workers' Fairness Act (employers with 15+ employees) requires any paid or unpaid sick or disability leave an employer offers to cover pregnancy and childbirth, usable before and after birth or miscarriage. Employers must also discuss accommodations such as a modified schedule.
pregnancy_accommodation_law: Nevada requires employers with 15 or more employees to provide reasonable accommodations for conditions related to pregnancy, childbirth or related medical conditions, including lactation, unless it causes undue hardship. The employer must work out the accommodation with you in a timely, good-faith process and can't force leave if an accommodation would let you keep working (Nevada Pregnant Workers' Fairness Act, NRS 613.4353 to 613.4383, 2017).
lactation_at_work_law: Nevada requires employers to give employees with a child under 1 reasonable break time, paid or unpaid, to pump, plus a private place that isn't a bathroom. Employers with fewer than 50 workers are exempt if it would cause undue hardship, and a parallel law covers public employers (NRS 608.0193 and 281.755, 2017).
state_employee_parental_leave: Nevada gives executive-branch state employees with 12 straight months of service 8 weeks of paid family leave at 50% of regular pay, which can be used to bond with a newborn or newly adopted child. Employees must have at least 40 hours of sick leave and use any sick leave above 40 hours first (NRS 284.356, 2023).
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: No voluntary paid family leave insurance law found as of October 2026.

program_name: Granite State Paid Family Leave Plan (New Hampshire Paid Family and Medical Leave, NH PFML), insured by MetLife
summary: New Hampshire has no required paid leave. You're paid only if your employer buys the Granite State plan or you buy an individual plan well ahead of time (60% of wages for 6 weeks, after a 7-month wait).
wage_replacement: 60% of your average weekly wage (based on the last four completed calendar quarters), with wages capped at the Social Security wage base ($184,500 in 2026); max $2,128.85/week in 2026. Only if you are enrolled: through an employer that buys the plan, or by buying an individual plan yourself.
waiting_period: Employer plans: a one-time 7-day unpaid waiting period each benefit year. Individual plan: a one-time 7-month waiting period after enrollment before benefits are available, plus a one-week elimination period.
job_protection: NH PFML pays benefits only; it does not protect your job (MetLife). Separate laws may: federal FMLA (50+ employees, 12 months/1,250 hours, 12 weeks unpaid); NH RSA 354-A:7 VI (employers with 6+ employees must allow unpaid leave for the period you are physically disabled by pregnancy or childbirth, then return you to your job or a comparable one unless business necessity prevents it); and, from Jan. 1, 2026, RSA 275:37-f (employers with 20+ employees must allow up to 25 hours of unpaid leave in the child's first year for childbirth, postpartum and pediatric appointments, with your job held).
eligibility: Voluntary. State employees are covered automatically. Any employer with a physical NH location may buy group coverage (6 or 12 weeks). If your employer offers NH PFML and you decline it, you cannot buy individual coverage. If your employer does not offer NH PFML or an equivalent plan, you can buy an individual plan (up to 6 weeks; premium capped at $5/week) during the state's 60-day annual open enrollment. You must work for an employer with an NH location (remote workers count); gig workers, contractors and people who are not employed are not eligible.
state_leave_laws: Employers with 6+ employees must let you take leave while you're physically unable to work because of pregnancy, childbirth or a related condition, then give you back your job or a comparable one unless business necessity makes that impossible or unreasonable (RSA 354-A:7 VI). Since Jan. 1, 2026, employers with 20+ employees must also allow up to 25 hours of unpaid leave in your baby's first year for your childbirth and postpartum appointments and the baby's pediatric visits, with your job held (RSA 275:37-f). Neither law requires pay.
pregnancy_accommodation_law: No state pregnancy accommodation law found as of October 2026. State law does require employers with 6+ employees to allow leave while you're physically disabled by pregnancy or childbirth (RSA 354-A:7 VI).
lactation_at_work_law: Since July 1, 2025, New Hampshire employers with 6+ employees in the state, including state and local government, must give unpaid breaks of about 30 minutes for every 3 hours worked to pump, for 1 year after birth, plus a clean, private space within a reasonable walk that isn't a bathroom. Employers must have a written policy, you must give 2 weeks' notice, and an employer can be exempted for undue hardship (RSA 275:78-83; 2023 law).
state_employee_parental_leave: New Hampshire gives permanent state employees paid family leave at no cost to them: 60% of their average weekly wage for up to 6 weeks a year, including for a birth and newborn care within a year or an adoption or foster placement. It has been in place since Jan. 1, 2023 (RSA 21-I:102, 21-I:111; 2021 law). The law's required coverage leaves out the employee's own health condition, such as recovery from childbirth.
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: New Hampshire's Granite State Paid Family Leave Plan is a voluntary state plan insured by MetLife and available since Jan. 1, 2023: employers can buy group coverage, and workers whose employer doesn't offer it can buy an individual plan through a state pool with premiums capped at $5 a week, a 60-day annual enrollment window and a 7-month waiting period. The statutory benefit is 60% of average weekly wages for up to 6 weeks a year (RSA 21-I:99 to 21-I:111 and RSA 282-B; 2021 law). HB 1761 (2026), which would have expanded the program, was sent to interim study.

program_name: New Jersey Temporary Disability Insurance (TDI) and Family Leave Insurance (FLI)
summary: New Jersey pays 85% of wages, up to $1,119 a week in 2026: Temporary Disability Insurance for pregnancy and recovery (typically 10 to 12 weeks), then up to 12 weeks of Family Leave Insurance to bond.
pregnancy_recovery_typical: NJ says TDI is usually payable up to 4 weeks before your expected delivery date and up to 6 weeks after birth (8 weeks after a C-section). It can last longer if your provider certifies complications. NJ describes this as typically 10–12 weeks of TDI, followed by up to 12 weeks of FLI bonding.
wage_replacement: 85% of your average weekly wage, up to a maximum of $1,119/week in 2026 ($1,081 in 2025). The same max applies to TDI and FLI.
waiting_period: TDI has a 7-day 'waiting week'. NJ pays from the 8th day, and pays the first 7 days retroactively once your leave reaches 22 days, which a pregnancy claim normally does. FLI bonding has no waiting period.
job_protection: Yes, as of July 17, 2026 (P.L.2025, c.279). If you receive TDI or FLI benefits and your leave isn't already covered by the NJ Family Leave Act, the TDI/FLI law entitles you to your same or an equivalent job when leave ends. There is no minimum employer size or work-history requirement. The NJ Family Leave Act (12 weeks of job-protected bonding leave in 24 months) now covers employers with 15+ employees, down from 30+, and employees with 3 months and 250 hours on the job, down from 12 months and 1,000 hours. Federal FMLA (50+ employees, 12 months, 1,250 hours) can also protect pregnancy and childbirth recovery.
eligibility: For 2026 claims you must have worked 20 base weeks earning at least $310/week, or earned at least $15,500 total, in the base year (first 4 of the last 5 completed quarters). Most NJ private and public employees are covered. Federal employees, out-of-state employees, and contractors who aren't employees are not; local government is optional for TDI. TDI can be paid by the state or by your employer's approved private plan. FLI bonding must be used within the child's first year.

lactation_at_work_law: New Mexico requires every employer, including state and local government, to give nursing employees flexible break times and a clean, private space near their work area that isn't a bathroom to use a breast pump. Employers don't have to pay for pumping time beyond regular breaks (HB 613, 2007, NMSA ch. 28, art. 20).
state_employee_parental_leave: New Mexico gives eligible executive-branch state employees up to 12 weeks of fully paid parental leave, used within six months of a birth or adoption, after they finish a probationary or one-year service period (Executive Order 2019-036, in effect since Jan. 1, 2020, amended 2020).
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: No voluntary paid family leave insurance law found as of October 2026.

program_name: New York Paid Family Leave (PFL) and Disability Benefits Law (DBL) short-term disability
summary: New York pays up to 12 weeks of Paid Family Leave to bond at 67% of wages (max $1,228.53 a week in 2026); disability benefits for pregnancy and recovery pay only 50%, up to $170 a week.
pregnancy_recovery_typical: WCB says DBL pays a pregnant worker for 4 weeks before the due date and 6 weeks after birth (8 weeks after a C-section). It can extend up to 26 weeks with documentation from your provider. PFL bonding starts after birth and can't be paid at the same time as DBL.
wage_replacement: PFL (bonding): 67% of your average weekly wage, up to 67% of the NY State average weekly wage: max $1,228.53/week in 2026. DBL (your own pregnancy/childbirth disability): 50% of your average weekly wage for the last 8 weeks worked, max only $170/week.
waiting_period: DBL: 7-day unpaid waiting period; benefits start on the 8th consecutive day of disability. PFL bonding: no waiting period.
job_protection: PFL is job-protected: after PFL you're entitled to your same or a comparable job with the same benefits and pay. The law sets no employer-size test; the 26-week/175-day eligibility rule applies. DBL time for your own pregnancy or childbirth recovery has no job protection under the DBL law, so federal FMLA (50+ employees, 12 months, 1,250 hours) is the main protection for that period. NY law also bars retaliation for taking legally protected absences.
eligibility: PFL: you must be employed by a covered NY employer, working 20+ hours/week for 26 consecutive weeks or fewer than 20 hours/week for 175 days worked. Most private employers must carry DBL and PFL. Public employers and self-employed people can opt in. Construction workers under a CBA get an alternative test starting in 2027. DBL: eligible after 4 consecutive weeks with a covered employer, and you must be under the care of a physician, certified nurse midwife or other listed provider. Claims go through your employer's insurance carrier, not the state.

It doesn't cover private employers or local governments (Executive Order 82, 2018).

Private employers aren't covered by a state law, so federal PUMP Act rules apply (State Human Resources Lactation Support Policy, updated 2024; Executive Order 82).
state_employee_parental_leave: North Carolina gives state employees up to 8 weeks of paid leave after giving birth and up to 4 weeks for other new parents, including through adoption or foster care. It covers state agencies, the UNC system, public schools and community colleges, and part-time staff get a prorated amount (N.C. Gen. Stat. 126-8.6, 2023).
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: No voluntary paid family leave insurance law found as of October 2026. Bills for a state-run program (H 499 and S 480) have sat in committee since March 2025.

If the employer has no leave policy, it must still allow the leave and reinstate you to your original job or one of like status and pay. No set length or pay is required.

Private employers follow the federal PUMP Act.

They can use their own leave to bring pay up to 100%, and the leave must be taken within a year (Ohio Rev. Code 124.136, expanded in 2023).
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: No voluntary paid family leave insurance law found as of October 2026. A bill to allow it (HB 593) passed the Ohio House in June 2026 and is waiting in a Senate committee.

For private employers the law only says they may offer unpaid breaks, so federal PUMP Act rules apply.

Full-time public school employees with a year of service also get 6 weeks of paid maternity leave (70 O.S. § 6-104.8, 2023).
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: No voluntary paid family leave insurance law found as of October 2026.

program_name: Paid Leave Oregon (Oregon Paid Family and Medical Leave Insurance)
summary: Oregon pays up to 12 weeks for recovery and bonding combined, plus 2 more weeks for pregnancy (14 total), at up to 100% of wages, max $1,692.16 a week for claims from June 28, 2026.
wage_replacement: 100% of your average weekly wage if you earn 65% or less of the state average weekly wage; above that, 65% of the state average weekly wage plus 50% of your wages above that amount. Max $1,692.16/week for benefit years starting on or after June 28, 2026 ($1,636.56 if your benefit year started earlier); min $70.51.
waiting_period: None (no waiting week for any leave type)
job_protection: Yes, in the Paid Leave law itself, for employees who have worked at least 90 consecutive days for the employer, at employers of any size. You get your same job back; if it no longer exists, employers with 25+ employees must offer an equivalent job (within 50 miles), and employers with fewer than 25 may give a different job with similar duties and the same pay and benefits. Health insurance continues during leave. Leave runs at the same time as federal FMLA when both apply; the Oregon Family Leave Act (OFLA, unpaid) separately covers some other reasons such as bereavement.
eligibility: You must work for an employer in Oregon and have earned at least $1,000 in wages in your base year (or alternate base year), with no minimum time on the job to get benefits. Covers full-time, part-time and seasonal workers of nearly all employers. Self-employed people, independent contractors and Tribal government employers can opt in. Not covered: federal employees and some other excluded groups.

summary: Pennsylvania has no state paid family leave program, so paid time off after birth depends on your employer; federal FMLA gives eligible workers 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave.
wage_replacement: No state paid family leave program.
job_protection: Federal FMLA gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if the employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you've worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. No Pennsylvania law sets a required amount of pregnancy or parental leave beyond federal FMLA. State Human Relations Commission rules (employers with 4+ workers) say leave, extension and reinstatement policies must apply to pregnancy and childbirth recovery on the same terms as other temporary disabilities.
state_leave_laws: No Pennsylvania law sets a required amount of pregnancy or parental leave beyond federal FMLA. State Human Relations Commission rules (employers with 4+ workers) say leave, extension and reinstatement policies must apply to pregnancy and childbirth recovery on the same terms as other temporary disabilities.
pregnancy_accommodation_law: No state pregnancy accommodation law found as of October 2026. Philadelphia and Pittsburgh have their own local accommodation laws.
lactation_at_work_law: Pennsylvania has no lactation law for private employers. A Commonwealth HR policy gives employees of state agencies under the Governor reasonable break time to pump for up to 2 years after a birth, and a private space with a lock that isn't a restroom (HR-WS001, effective Jan. 4, 2024). State rules also require a nursing mothers' room in new Commonwealth-owned and leased buildings (4 Pa. Code ch. 67c, 2018). Private employers follow the federal PUMP Act.
state_employee_parental_leave: Pennsylvania gives Commonwealth employees who meet FMLA eligibility rules up to 8 weeks of paid parental leave for a birth, adoption or foster placement on or after Feb. 15, 2024 (6 weeks for events from Oct. 15, 2020). It covers management and non-union staff, plus union members whose unions agreed to it. Commonwealth policy also allows up to 6 months of paid and unpaid parental and family absence, with benefits, in a rolling year (Management Directive 530.30).
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: No voluntary paid family leave insurance law found as of October 2026.

program_name: Rhode Island Temporary Disability Insurance (TDI) and Temporary Caregiver Insurance (TCI)
summary: Rhode Island pays about 60% of wages, up to $1,150 a week for claims from July 1, 2026: disability insurance for pregnancy and recovery, then up to 8 weeks of caregiver insurance to bond, within a 30-week yearly cap.
wage_replacement: 4.62% of your wages in the highest-paid quarter of your base period (about 60% of weekly pay), up to $1,150/week for claims from July 1, 2026 ($1,103 for January to June 2026). Dependents' allowances are added on top: the greater of $20 or 7% of your rate per dependent child, up to 5, for a max of $1,552/week. The rate rises to 5.38% of high-quarter wages for benefit years starting in 2027 and 5.77% from 2028.
waiting_period: No unpaid waiting week; the waiting-period statute (§ 28-41-12) was repealed. You must be out of work for at least 7 consecutive days to qualify for TDI (§ 28-41-11(c)).
job_protection: TCI (bonding) leave is job-protected by the TCI law itself (§ 28-41-35(f)): you return to your same or an equivalent position, and your employer must keep your health benefits during the leave. The TCI law sets no employer-size or tenure test. TDI (your own pregnancy or childbirth disability) has no job protection under the TDI law. For that time, look to the RI Parental and Family Medical Leave Act (employers with 50+ employees; full-time employees averaging 30+ hours/week with 12 consecutive months; 13 weeks in 2 calendar years) or federal FMLA.
eligibility: You must have paid into TDI through RI covered employment and met a base-period earnings test tied to the RI minimum wage ($16.00/hour in 2026). That means either $19,200 in base-period wages, or $3,200 in one quarter plus total base-period wages of at least 1.5 times your highest quarter and at least $6,400. TCI bonding is for a newborn, adopted or foster child, and you must give your employer 30 days' written notice when possible. Private plans are not allowed in RI.

program_name: Voluntary paid family leave insurance (employer-purchased)
summary: South Carolina has no state paid family leave program. A 2024 law lets insurers sell paid family leave policies to employers, so you're covered only if your employer buys one.
wage_replacement: Set by each policy; only if your employer buys coverage.
waiting_period: Set by each policy (the law only requires the policy to say whether there is an unpaid waiting period).
job_protection: This law does not protect your job. The federal FMLA may: up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if your employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you have worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. We found no state law that adds job-protected leave for private-sector workers.
eligibility: Only employees (people for whom the employer completes a Form I-9; not independent contractors) whose employer buys a family leave insurance policy or rider; eligibility rules are set by the policy. No state-run program.
law_citation: Paid Family Leave Insurance Act, S.C. Code §§ 38-103-10 to 38-103-90; 2024 Act No. 206 (H.4832), effective May 21, 2024
state_leave_laws: No state law beyond federal FMLA was found.
pregnancy_accommodation_law: South Carolina's Pregnancy Accommodations Act (2018) requires employers with 15+ employees to make reasonable accommodations for medical needs from pregnancy, childbirth or related conditions, including lactation, unless it causes undue hardship. Examples include more frequent breaks, seating, help with lifting, a temporary transfer and schedule changes, and employers must give workers written notice of these rights (S.C. Code §§ 1-13-30, 1-13-80).
lactation_at_work_law: South Carolina's Lactation Support Act (2020) covers every employer with 1+ employees, including state and local government: it must give reasonable unpaid break time, or let you use paid breaks or meal time, to pump each day, and make reasonable efforts to provide a private place near your work area that isn't a toilet stall. An employer doesn't have to provide break time if it would cause undue hardship (S.C. Code § 41-1-130).
state_employee_parental_leave: South Carolina state employees who give birth (including a stillbirth) get 6 weeks of paid leave at 100% of base pay, used within 12 months; the other parent gets 4 weeks for births on or after Oct. 1, 2026, up from 2. The benefit started in 2022 (S.C. Code § 8-11-150), public school district employees got it to the same extent in 2023 (§ 8-11-151), and Act 249 of 2026 raised the second parent's weeks.
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: South Carolina's Paid Family Leave Insurance Act lets life and disability income insurers sell family leave coverage to employers as a rider to, or part of, a group disability or life policy, or as a separate group policy. Covered reasons include bonding in the first 12 months after a birth, adoption or foster placement, and policies must pay at least 2 weeks per covered reason in a 52-week period. It took effect May 21, 2024 (S.C. Code §§ 38-103-10 to 38-103-90; Act 206 of 2024, H.4832).

Tennessee's Parental Leave Act lets full-time employees at a job site with 100+ full-time workers take up to 4 months of leave for pregnancy, childbirth, nursing an infant or adoption, after 12 consecutive months. Pay is the employer's choice. Give 3 months' notice (medical emergencies excepted) to keep your right to return.
eligibility: Only employees (people for whom the employer completes a Form I-9; not independent contractors) whose employer buys a family leave insurance policy or rider; eligibility rules are set by the policy. No state-run program.
law_citation: Tennessee Paid Family Leave Insurance Act, Tenn. Code Ann. Title 56, Chapter 7 (new part); 2023 Public Chapter No. 91 (SB 454 / HB 609, 113th General Assembly), signed March 31, 2023; effective Jan. 1, 2024 for policies entered into, amended or renewed on or after that date
state_leave_laws: Tennessee's Parental Leave Act lets full-time employees at a job site with 100+ full-time workers take up to 4 months of leave for pregnancy, childbirth, nursing an infant or adoption, after 12 consecutive months. Pay is the employer's choice. Give 3 months' notice (medical emergencies excepted) to keep your right to return.
pregnancy_accommodation_law: Tennessee requires employers with 15 or more employees to make reasonable accommodations for medical needs arising from pregnancy, childbirth or related conditions unless it causes undue hardship, such as more frequent breaks, lifting limits or a temporary transfer. Employers can't force you onto leave if another accommodation would work (Tennessee Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, Tenn. Code 50-10-101 to -104, in effect since Oct. 1, 2020).
lactation_at_work_law: Tennessee requires employers to give reasonable unpaid break time each day to pump for an infant, unless it would unduly disrupt operations, and to make reasonable efforts to provide a private place near the work area that isn't a toilet stall (Tenn. Code 50-1-305). Employers with 15 or more workers may also have to provide a private, non-bathroom space to pump as a pregnancy accommodation (2020).

It must be used within 12 months (2023 Tenn. Pub. Acts ch. 216, effective July 1, 2023).

Employers choose whether to buy it (Tennessee Paid Family Leave Insurance Act, Tenn. Code Title 56, Ch. 7; 2023 Pub. Ch. 91, effective Jan. 1, 2024).

state_leave_laws: No state law beyond federal FMLA was found.
pregnancy_accommodation_law: Texas requires cities and counties to make a reasonable effort to accommodate an employee whose doctor finds her partially restricted by pregnancy, and to give her an available temporary assignment in the same office if she can't do her regular job. The law covers only city and county employees, not private employers (Tex. Local Gov't Code § 180.004, 2001).
lactation_at_work_law: Texas requires public employers (state agencies, public colleges, cities, counties, school districts and other local governments) to give reasonable break time and a private place, other than a multi-user bathroom, to pump, and to adopt a written lactation policy (Tex. Gov't Code ch. 619, 2015). Private employers aren't required to; they can choose to earn the state's "mother-friendly" designation (Tex. Health & Safety Code § 165.003).

It covers executive-branch agency employees (not public colleges and universities) and other Employees Retirement System members (Tex. Gov't Code § 661.9125, 2023). Employees not yet eligible for FMLA can take up to 12 weeks of parental leave, unpaid once accrued leave runs out (§ 661.913).

You're covered only if your employer buys a policy (Tex. Ins. Code ch. 1255, effective Sept. 1, 2023).

summary: Utah has no state paid family leave program, so paid time off after birth depends on your employer; federal FMLA gives eligible workers 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave.

state_leave_laws: No state law beyond federal FMLA was found.
pregnancy_accommodation_law: Utah requires employers with 15 or more employees, plus state and local government, to provide reasonable accommodations for pregnancy, childbirth, breastfeeding and related conditions unless it would cause undue hardship. Employers can't demand a doctor's note for more frequent restroom, food or water breaks (Utah Code § 34A-5-106, 2016).

Private employers with 15 or more employees must reasonably accommodate breastfeeding under the state's 2016 pregnancy accommodation law.
