An employee who gives birth first gets up to 6 work weeks of paid postpartum recovery leave, up from 3 weeks before July 1, 2026, for up to 9 paid weeks in all (Utah Code § 63A-17-511; enacted 2022, expanded by H.B. 329 in 2026).
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: No voluntary paid family leave insurance law found as of October 2026. Bills to add family leave insurance to Utah's insurance code failed in 2024 and 2025.

program_name: Vermont Family and Medical Leave Insurance (VT FMLI), insured and administered by The Hartford
summary: Vermont has no required paid leave. The voluntary VT FMLI plan pays 60% of wages for up to 6 weeks if your employer buys it or you enroll yourself (enroll in May; benefits start the next January).
wage_replacement: 60% of your average weekly wage up to a maximum weekly benefit tied to the Social Security wage base; max $2,128.85/week for 2026 claims under the state-employee plan. The Hartford's individual-plan page still lists $2,031.92. Only if you are enrolled: through an employer that buys VT FMLI, or by buying individual coverage yourself. Employer plans can offer 60-70%.
waiting_period: 7 calendar days at the start of each claim, waived when bonding leave immediately follows a childbirth medical claim. Individual plan: enroll May 1-31, coverage starts July 1, then a 6-month eligibility waiting period, so benefits are first available the following January 1.
job_protection: VT FMLI pays benefits only; it does not protect your job. Separate laws may: Vermont's Parental and Family Leave Act (21 V.S.A. § 472) gives up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected parental leave a year (including pregnancy and, since July 1, 2025, recovery from childbirth or miscarriage) at employers with 10+ employees for employees with 1 year at an average of 30+ hours/week; the federal FMLA also applies at employers with 50+ employees.
eligibility: Voluntary. State of Vermont employees are covered by the state plan. Employers with a Vermont location and 2+ employees may buy group coverage (they design it: 6-26 weeks, 60-70% pay). Individuals can buy the 6-week individual plan if they live and work in Vermont and their employer doesn't offer FMLI, or if they are a self-employed Vermont resident; one-employee employers also use the individual pool. Annual enrollment is May 1-31; special enrollment within 30 days of losing employer coverage, changing jobs, or moving to Vermont.
state_leave_laws: Vermont's Parental and Family Leave Act gives up to 12 weeks a year of unpaid, job-protected leave for pregnancy, recovery from childbirth or miscarriage, and bonding with a new child in its first year, at employers with 10+ employees who work an average of 30+ hours a week. You qualify after 1 year with the employer averaging 30+ hours a week; your benefits continue and you get the same or a comparable job back (21 V.S.A. §§ 471-472; childbirth and miscarriage recovery added by Act 32 of 2025).
pregnancy_accommodation_law: Since Jan. 1, 2018, every Vermont employer with at least 1 employee must provide reasonable accommodations for pregnancy-related conditions unless it would cause undue hardship, using the same standards as disability accommodations, and must post a notice of the law (21 V.S.A. § 495k; Act 21 of 2017).
lactation_at_work_law: For 3 years after a birth, every Vermont employer must give nursing employees reasonable time during the day to pump (paid or unpaid, at the employer's choice) and a private space that isn't a bathroom stall. An employer can be exempted only if this would substantially disrupt its operations (21 V.S.A. § 305, enacted 2008).
state_employee_parental_leave: State of Vermont employees (classified or exempt, in the executive, judicial and legislative branches) with at least 1 year of service are automatically enrolled in VT FMLI, which pays 60% of base weekly wages for up to 6 combined weeks a year, including for childbirth recovery and bonding with a new child. The state pays the full premium, and benefits began July 1, 2023.
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: Vermont's voluntary plan, VT FMLI, insured by The Hartford, was created by Gov. Phil Scott's administration through a state contract rather than a statute. It covered state employees from July 2023, employers with 2+ employees could buy plans from July 2024 (6-26 weeks at 60-70% pay), and individuals and self-employed Vermonters could enroll from 2025, with benefits from Jan. 1, 2026. The 2025-2026 legislature passed no paid leave law; its only leave act (Act 32 of 2025) expanded unpaid leave.

program_name: Virginia Paid Family and Medical Leave Insurance Program (PFML), administered by the Virginia Employment Commission
summary: Virginia passed paid family and medical leave in April 2026, but benefits don't start until December 1, 2028: up to 12 weeks a year at 80% of wages.
wage_replacement: When benefits start Dec. 1, 2028: 80% of your average weekly wage (your full wage if you earn under $100/week), min $100/week, max equal to 100% of the state average weekly wage, set each year. The 2028 dollar cap hasn't been published. No benefits are paid in 2026.
waiting_period: None for employees (benefits payable from the first day you're eligible in a benefit year). Self-employed people who opt in more than 26 weeks after becoming self-employed must wait 52 weeks before benefits are paid.
job_protection: Yes, in the new law: if you've worked for your current employer at least 120 days before leave, you must be restored to your job or one with equivalent seniority, status, pay, benefits and service credits, and health coverage continues during leave. Retaliation, including immigration-status threats, is prohibited. Until benefits begin in Dec. 2028, only federal FMLA (50+ employees, 12 months/1,250 hours) gives job-protected leave.
eligibility: You'll need to meet Virginia's minimum earnings test for unemployment insurance (wages in your two highest base-period quarters at least the lowest amount in the UI benefit table, earned in at least 2 quarters) and be authorized to work in the U.S. Covers nearly all private and local-government employers, including small businesses (10 or fewer employees don't pay the employer share). State employees get equal or better leave through state HR policy instead. Self-employed people can opt in for at least 3 years.

program_name: Washington Paid Family and Medical Leave
summary: Washington pays up to 12 weeks to bond plus medical leave for pregnancy and recovery, up to 16 weeks combined (18 with a complication such as a C-section), at up to 90% of wages, max $1,647 a week in 2026.
pregnancy_recovery_typical: Washington automatically treats the first 6 weeks after you give birth (the 'postnatal period') as medical leave. You don't need a medical certification and there's no waiting week, just proof of birth. Leave before birth for pregnancy incapacity needs a medical certification and has a waiting week. You can then add family leave to bond, up to 16 weeks total, or 18 if you had a pregnancy complication causing incapacity (ESD's examples are bed rest or a C-section).
wage_replacement: 90% of your average weekly wage up to half the state average weekly wage, plus 50% of the amount above that. Minimum $100/week; maximum $1,647/week in 2026 ($1,542 in 2025). Your max is locked in for the claim year you start.
waiting_period: No waiting week for bonding leave or for leave taken in the 6-week postnatal period. Medical leave taken before birth, for example pregnancy bed rest, has a 7-day unpaid waiting week.
job_protection: The PFML law itself protects your job (RCW 50A.35.010) if you've worked for your employer at least 180 calendar days and it has 25 or more employees in 2026. That threshold drops to 15+ in 2027 and 8+ from 2028; there's no hours requirement. Your employer must restore you to the same or an equivalent job and, starting 2026, keep your health coverage. Exceptions: the top 10% of salaried earners (if restoring them would cause serious financial harm and they get notice), and jobs that would not have existed anyway. Without PFML job protection, federal FMLA or other laws may apply.
eligibility: You must have worked 820 hours in Washington in your qualifying period, normally the first 4 of the last 5 completed calendar quarters. If that doesn't get you to 820 hours, ESD uses the last 4 completed quarters before you apply instead. Full-time, part-time, temporary and seasonal work all count, and you don't need to be currently employed. Workers at businesses of all sizes are covered. Not covered: federal employees, tribal-business employees on tribal land, workers on an approved employer voluntary plan (who apply through that plan), and self-employed people who haven't opted in.

summary: West Virginia has no state paid family leave program, so paid time off after birth depends on your employer; federal FMLA gives eligible workers 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave.
wage_replacement: No state paid family leave program.
job_protection: Federal FMLA gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave if the employer has 50+ employees within 75 miles and you've worked there 12 months and 1,250 hours. We found no state law that adds job-protected leave for private-sector workers.
state_leave_laws: No state law beyond federal FMLA was found.
pregnancy_accommodation_law: West Virginia's Pregnant Workers' Fairness Act requires the state, local governments and employers with 12 or more employees to make reasonable accommodations for limitations from pregnancy, childbirth or related conditions once the worker provides a health care provider's written note, unless it would cause undue hardship (W. Va. Code § 16B-19-2; passed 2014, renumbered 2024).
lactation_at_work_law: No state lactation-at-work law found as of October 2026. Federal PUMP Act rules apply.
state_employee_parental_leave: No state-employee paid parental leave law found as of October 2026. State and county school board employees can take 12 weeks of unpaid leave for a birth or adoption after using up their annual and personal leave (W. Va. Code § 21-5D-4).
voluntary_pfl_insurance_law: No voluntary paid family leave insurance law found as of October 2026.

Permanent classified state employees can take up to 6 months of unpaid maternity, paternity or adoption leave, which the agency may extend by up to 6 more months, and may use accrued sick leave for medical recovery from birth (Wisconsin Human Resources Handbook ch. 740, revised 2018).
